analysis.one_liner: Reinstates expired taxes on oil and chemical companies to fund toxic-waste cleanup.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the House Ways and Means Committee from April 2011 until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bring back two Superfund taxes that Congress let expire in 1995: a per-barrel fee on crude oil and petroleum products and a small corporate tax on very large companies, both earmarked for the Superfund trust fund that pays to clean up the nation's worst toxic-waste sites. The idea is that the companies whose products created the contamination, not ordinary taxpayers, should finance those cleanups.
analysis.who_benefits: Communities living near Superfund sites, which get a better-funded cleanup program, and general taxpayers, who currently bear cleanup costs through regular government spending when the industry-funded trust runs short.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents near toxic sites and taxpayers

how_it_helps.text: Reinstates the Hazardous Substance Superfund financing rate, an excise tax on crude oil and petroleum products, through the end of 2018, with the revenue flowing to the Superfund trust fund that pays for cleaning up hazardous-waste sites.
Reinstates the corporate environmental income tax, a tax on very large corporations, through the end of 2018, also directed to Superfund financing.
Implements the 'polluter pays' principle: instead of cleaning up toxic sites with general taxpayer money, the industries whose products created the hazardous substances would fund the program.

analysis.who_pays: Oil companies importing or producing crude oil and petroleum products, chemical-related businesses, and very large corporations that would pay the reinstated environmental income tax; some of the excise cost would be passed to consumers at the pump.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and chemical companies and large corporations

drawbacks.text: An excise tax on crude oil is partly passed through to consumers in the price of gasoline and petroleum products, so households would bear some of the cost despite the polluter-pays label.

The corporate environmental income tax applies broadly to very large corporations rather than only to companies responsible for contaminated sites, meaning some firms that pollute little would still pay.

Reinstating federal taxes on energy inputs could raise production costs for U.S. manufacturers at a time when supporters of letting the taxes lapse had argued the fees burdened American industry relative to foreign competitors.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a dedicated funding stream for cleaning up toxic-waste sites, with the cost borne mainly by oil, chemical, and other large companies rather than taxpayers. The honest trade-off is that some of the excise tax reaches consumers through fuel prices, and the corporate tax hits large firms generally rather than polluters specifically. On balance the bill shifts a public cleanup burden back onto the industries whose products generated it.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, which took no action on it — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone introduced the Superfund Polluter Pays Act on April 15, 2011, with Rep. Earl Blumenauer as the sole cosponsor.
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over taxes.
That was the last action ever recorded: over the rest of the 112th Congress the committee held no markup and the House never voted on the bill.
Congress had allowed both Superfund taxes to expire at the end of 1995, and this bill would have revived them from enactment through January 1, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and chemical companies avoided having the Superfund taxes reinstated, and the cleanup burden continued to fall on general taxpayers and on the Superfund program's limited budget. Communities near toxic sites gained nothing from the bill's failure.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and chemical companies; taxpayers kept the bill

for.name: Rep. Frank Pallone, Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Superfund Polluter Pays Act on April 15, 2011.

for.name: Rep. Earl Blumenauer
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, the only cosponsor it attracted.

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican in the 112th Congress
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill on the day of introduction and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, and no vote was ever scheduled in the House.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's two sponsors were both Democrats and it had no Republican support on paper, but since it never reached a floor vote the actual partisan split was never tested.

industries.note: The bill would reinstate a per-barrel excise tax on crude oil and petroleum products that these companies have not paid since 1995; their interest in keeping the tax off runs against the public's interest in a funded cleanup program.

industries.industry: Chemical and other companies using hazardous substances
industries.note: Reinstating the Superfund financing rate raises costs for businesses whose products are the source of the hazardous substances Superfund cleans up.
The corporate environmental income tax would apply again to very large companies' taxable income through 2018, a broad tax not limited to firms with contaminated sites.

Since the industry taxes lapsed in 1995, Superfund cleanups have relied on general revenues from ordinary taxpayers; restoring the polluter-paid trust fund would relieve that burden but the program would also gain a dedicated funding stream.
